transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-16
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Lucas Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Alvarez (CatalystFin Eng Mgr), Priya Nair (CatalystFin SRE Lead), Omar Sheikh (CatalystFin Head of Platform)

Summary:
Post-incident transition call to move from containment to prevention. Discussed root cause hypothesis (KV cache eviction combined with a subtle mem growth), short-term mitigations, longer-term regression guardrails, canary and SLA rebuild plan, and runbook ownership. Agreement to run joint load tests and deliver tuning docs.

Topics:
- Incident recap and customer impact
- What containment worked, what failed
- Short-term fixes (autoscale, TTLs, fallback throttles)
- Long-term prevention (memory hardening, regression tests, monitoring)
- Ownership and schedule for runbook + canary

Action items (captured above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: okay everyone thanks for joining, uh we wanted to get this on right away so we can hand off from the initial firefight into a prevention sprint, um hi Jordan, Priya, Omar.
[00:18] Jordan: hey thanks, yeah appreciate it, we, as you know, had a pretty bad SLA blip last Thursday, err, it was rough for the payments path.
[00:25] Priya: yeah lots of error spikes, and the alerts screamed for a few mins before our fallback triggered which made the whole thing visible to many users.
[00:33] Lucas: quick callout from our side — we collected heap dumps and KV cache metrics, and there's a pattern showing progressive resident set growth on the worker nodes that aligned with heavy sequence lengths.
[00:42] Omar: when you say "sequence lengths" do you mean longer prompts or more tokens per request?
[00:47] Lucas: mostly longer token windows; a batch of deals came in with very long transcripts. The cache entries were sticking because TTLs were effectively infinite for certain keys under the old config.
[00:56] Jordan: that matches what we saw — a particular customer integration sent a flood of chat-history-heavy payloads. We also have some legacy prefetching code that pins contexts.
[01:06] Priya: the autoscaler didn't react fast enough because the CPU signal was flat while mem climbed, so we hit OOM eviction waves and worker restarts cascaded into increased latency.
[01:18] Maya: ok so containment was partial: the fallback path caught some traffic but it was noisy and caused partial timeouts. We need to codify what we did in the heat so it's repeatable.
[01:30] Lucas: for the quick fix we recommended a conservative mem limit and immediate TTLs on the KV entries; that reduced resident growth in our staging replay.
[01:38] Jordan: we applied the TTL patch in prod Friday night and saw an improvement but still a tail of long latencies until the restart window finished.
[01:46] Maya: right — so moving from containment to prevention, here's the proposed plan: 1) formalize a runbook with clear thresholds, 2) update autoscaler to consider mem pressure signal, 3) add regression tests that replay the specific long-token workload, 4) tighter KV cache defaults and eviction policy, 5) canary rollout for the new defaults.
[02:08] Priya: on the autoscaler point — can you walk through how Redwood would surface memory as a signal? We currently only get CPU and token throughput.
[02:16] Lucas: today our hosted nodes export memRSS, but the control plane doesn't consume it for scaling decisions; we can patch the scale controller to expose an aggregated mem p50/p90 and trigger scale-up when resident > threshold. There's some caveats around bursty GC though.
[02:29] Omar: sounds good, but we also need to be mindful of cost — CatalystFin has strict budget windows. Autoscaling more aggressively could double our reserved usage during spikes.
[02:39] Maya: yep totally — one of the goals is to balance cost vs risk. Our canary plan includes a cost cap and a gradual ramp that you control. We'll provide knobs to set a hard cap.
[02:49] Jordan: what's the risk of false positives? If mem spikes due to transient, I don't want the fleet to thrash.
[02:54] Lucas: fair, that's why we recommend a two-stage signal: mem > threshold for 30s AND queue depth rising; that helps avoid GC-induced blips.
[03:04] Priya: ok that seems reasonable. Also you mentioned the KV cache defaults — what specifically changed in the quick patch?
[03:10] Lucas: we set default TTL to 10m for new entries and added a max-entry-per-model guard; previously some models could pin unlimited contexts. The quick patch prevents unbounded growth but isn't tuned for optimal hit rates.
[03:22] Jordan: i'd like to see the tradeoffs — our hit-rate matters for token costs. If TTL too small we'll lose benefits.
[03:27] Maya: understood — part of the follow-up is a suggested matrix of TTLs by workload type; Lucas will produce that.
[03:34] Lucas: i'll include recommended numbers and a script to simulate hit-rate vs mem usage.
[03:38] Omar: another ask: can Redwood instrument the specific customer integration so we can see per-customer cache footprint?
[03:44] Lucas: yes we can add per-tenant metrics for cache entries and resident mem, anonymized if needed. That requires a small telemetry change but doable.
[03:51] Priya: legal might want anonymization — we'll flag that to Omar.
[03:55] Omar: yes, do that. Also, on the runbook ownership — who on Redwood side will be the primary contact for postmortem?
[04:00] Maya: Lucas will own the technical runbook authoring, I'll own the cross-functional communications and the SLA reconciliation.
[04:07] Jordan: good. Can we drill into the exact timeline and where the gaps were? I want the postmortem to be explicit.
[04:12] Maya: sure — we have a rough timeline and i'll upload annotated graphs; i'll also timestamp the key decisions (patch applied, restarts, fallback toggle).
[04:20] Lucas: note, there was also a correlated recluster that pushed rollout that day which increased connection churn. The two events combined amplified impact.
[04:29] Priya: oh right we had a minor deployment that overlapped, our deploy windows need better guardrail against heavy inference windows.
[04:35] Jordan: is Redwood able to suggest a maintenance gating system so we don't deploy during high queue windows?
[04:40] Lucas: we can provide an API to check current token throughput and queue length and gate deploys if above thresholds. Low lift.
[04:46] Maya: also discussed in the prep: we should add regression tests to CI that replay historical long-token flows and assert p95 < target. That will catch reintroductions.
[04:55] Priya: will those tests run on physical GPU-backed runners? If they run on cheap infra they won't surface mem growth in the same way.
[05:01] Lucas: agreed — they need to run on the same instance types (or at least same instance family) to be meaningful. We can supply a lightweight harness to run in your CI on a reserved test node.
[05:11] Jordan: ok we can budget that. Next — mitigation for live traffic: we had fallback throttles but they were too aggressive; suggestion to do gradual degrade per-customer rather than global toggle?
[05:21] Maya: that's in the plan: introduce per-tenant degraded mode thresholds and routing so we can shed the heaviest consumers first.
[05:28] Omar: how quickly can that be implemented? Our customers expect sub-200ms for some flows.
[05:33] Lucas: base implementation could be done in two sprints — first the per-tenant counters and a soft-shedding layer, then the policy engine for automated decisions. For immediate relief we can add a manual per-tenant throttle in the control plane.
[05:46] Priya: manual is fine short-term, we need automation medium-term.
[05:49] Jordan: what about observability — do you plan to add more traces for the fallback path so we can attribute errors precisely?
[05:55] Lucas: yes; we propose a single trace id that flows from router to worker to fallback; currently fallback loses some signals, we'll keep them intact.
[06:03] Maya: quick question — were there any security concerns during the incident? No data exfil, right?
[06:08] Omar: not that we saw, just elevated error rates and partial timeouts. Security fine.
[06:12] Priya: ok good.
[06:14] Maya: final part — SLA rebuild. Jordan, can you share the actual target windows and which endpoints are critical?
[06:20] Jordan: payments p95 and p99 are critical, we need p95 < 350ms normally, but during peak we're willing to accept p95 < 500ms for short windows.
[06:29] Maya: okay we'll model that in the canary plan. We'll create an acceptance criteria document for the canary that includes mem p90, p95 latency, and error-rate.
[06:38] Lucas: also recommend adding synthetic golden-requests that exercise long histories so canary includes that traffic shape.
[06:44] Jordan: agreed.
[06:46] Maya: timeline — immediate (this week): package artifacts, short patch rollout to TTL and mem hard limits, manual tenant throttles for the top 5 consumers. Next (1–2 weeks): autoscaler mem signal + per-tenant metrics + runbook draft. 2–4 weeks: canary, regression CI, and automation for shedding.
[07:04] Priya: that timeline seems plausible. We'll need sign-off from compliance on telemetry change which might take a few days.
[07:10] Omar: what about cost — is there an expectation that the canary or autoscale will spike monthly billing? We need runway.
[07:16] Maya: we'll include cost caps; the canary will be small percent of traffic and we can add automatic scale-down if cost overrun is detected.
[07:25] Jordan: ok, i want to confirm one more data point: you mentioned a memory leak hypothesis — is that confirmed or just correlated growth?
[07:31] Lucas: it's a correlation with the model variant we were using and the long token sequences — we saw an allocation pattern consistent with retention rather than just cache. We're still analyzing but the immediate mitigations don't require full fix first.
[07:45] Priya: if it's an allocation retention we might need a patch in the model runtime which will take longer. That influences whether autoscale is a durable solution.
[07:53] Lucas: agreed, and we'll prioritize a minimal runtime patch if needed; it's in our tracker as a medium priority item pending further dumps.
[08:00] Maya: okay, let's talk about who does what for the runbook rehearsal — proposed: Redwood runs the first rehearsal and invites CatalystFin ops to participate. We'll step through detection, thresholding, manual tenant throttle, and rollback.
[08:12] Jordan: good, schedule it early next week if possible.
[08:16] Maya: are there blockers to that?
[08:18] Priya: only calendar and ensuring we have a reserved test node for the reg tests.
[08:22] Lucas: we'll reserve one.
[08:24] Jordan: a couple quick clarifications: will Redwood's telemetry changes include per-tenant PII? Please confirm anonymization.
[08:30] Lucas: we will keep identifiers hashed and only expose aggregated metrics unless you opt-in for richer traces.
[08:36] Omar: good.
[08:38] Priya: two last items — please include a simple runbook exec checklist for on-call folks and add a one-page summary for exec stakeholders.
[08:46] Maya: yes, i'll draft an exec summary and Lucas will do the on-call checklist.
[08:50] Jordan: cool.
[08:52] Maya: anything else from you all?
[08:55] Omar: nope, just keep us in the loop.
[08:58] Priya: thanks everyone.
[09:00] Maya: wrap up — recap next steps and deadlines, then we'll close.
[09:06] Lucas: to restate: i'll produce TTL tuning doc and mem analysis by 2026-07-20; Maya to upload annotated timeline by 2026-07-18; both sides to run joint load next week and report results by 2026-07-23.
[09:23] Jordan: acknowledged.
[09:25] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up with links and schedule the rehearsal. Bye.
[52:00] End of recording.
